sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section questions why the manna was necessary to teach that man lives by God's utterance, since this should have been obvious after the Exodus and Splitting of the Sea.

translations.translation: Now, in Mishneh Torah,
it is written: "And He fed you the manna... in order to make known to you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every utterance of the mouth of G-d does man live."
That is to say, in addition to the aspect of the manna being "in order to test you, whether you will go in My Torah,"
there is another aspect in the manna,
which is "in order to make known to you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every utterance of the mouth of G-d does man live."
And the connection between these two aspects must be understood.
Furthermore, it requires explanation,
for seemingly there is a great and wondrous difficulty here:
Why is it necessary
(to come)
to have the manna in order to know that the entire existence is dependent upon the utterance of the mouth of G-d?
After all, it is seemingly a simple matter that "forever, O G-d, Your word stands firm in the heavens,"
meaning that the utterance of the mouth of G-d in every thing is what brings it into being, enlivens it, and sustains it,
and this matter is a simple faith for every single Jew, who are called "believers, children of believers," even while they were still in the land of Egypt,
all the more so after the Exodus from Egypt,
when the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself upon them in His glory and essence, etc.,
and especially after the Splitting of the Sea on the seventh day of Pesach, when they said, "This is my G-d and I will glorify Him,"
and if so, it is seemingly simple that "by every utterance of the mouth of G-d does man live,"
and what is the novel teaching of "Behold, I will rain down for you bread from heaven,"
and "He fed you the manna...", that specifically through this came the knowledge that "man does not live by bread alone, but by every utterance of the mouth of G-d does man live"?

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the novelty of the manna was not to teach that G-d sustains the world, but to reveal a higher level of Divine vitality beyond what was known from bread from the earth.

translations.translation: However, the general point of the explanation is this:
The novelty of "bread from heaven" came after there was the aspect of "bread from the earth" at its ultimate level,
and nevertheless, they say that there is a greater level in "bread from heaven"
(as will be explained later).
And similarly, regarding the novelty of "in order to make known to you that man does not live by bread alone,"
the intention is not to inform that the world is not, heaven forbid, in a state where there is no Master of this mansion and bread is an independent entity,
rather, this was known simply—that bread is brought into being from the utterance of G-d within it,
from the aspect of the Immanent Presence,
but this is still not the knowledge of the true essence of matters,
that "from the utterance of the mouth of G-d does man live."

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the spiritual difference between bread from heaven and bread from the earth, paralleling the distinction in divine service between Torah and mitzvos, and between Written and Oral Law.

translations.translation: And all this will be understood by first explaining the distinction between bread from heaven and bread from the earth as it is in the spirituality of the matter.
This is analogous to the distinction in divine service between Torah and mitzvos.
For the service of Torah is in a manner of drawing down from above to below,
"Is not My word like fire,"
and "I have placed My words in your mouth,"
meaning that this is the word of G-d that is drawn down below
(bread from heaven).
Therefore, changes do not apply to it, for the Torah is eternal.
However, the performance of mitzvos,
although this too comes through the study of Torah, as per the statement,
"Great is study that brings to action,"
nevertheless, it is connected to human action, that one must make from physical parchment the matter of tefillin,
and from physical wool the matter of tzitzis, etc.
(this is the aspect of "from the earth").
And with additional explanation, this will be understood from the two aspects as they are in the Torah itself
(for all matters of the world originate as they are in the Torah),
which are the Written Torah and the Oral Torah.
For in the Written Torah, every letter and every crownlet is precisely counted and enumerated,
and one cannot speak of addition or diminution, heaven forbid,
(from heaven),
however, regarding the Oral Torah it is written,
"It is longer than the measure of the earth and broader than the sea,"
and even to the extent of "and unnumbered worlds,"
without limit,
and this comes
through the toil of man
(from the earth),
"If you toiled and did not find, do not believe,"
for since he toils as required
(according to the demand of the Torah),
it is a clear matter that through this he has according to the manner of his toil,
even to the manner of "finding" and "you will find."
And just as it is in the line of Torah,
so too is it in the other two lines of gemilus chasadim
(mitzvos)
and divine service.
For there is this distinction
(in the line of gemilus chasadim)
between his spiritual service
(mitzvos)

and his service with the world, in a manner that requires toil of the soul and toil of the flesh in order to transform the world so that it becomes a dwelling place for Him, blessed be He, in the lower realms.
And similarly, there are these two aspects in divine service itself
(which is the intermediary between Torah and gemilus chasadim),
for there is the service of love with delights,
and likewise the service of the Shabbos day,
"and you shall call the Shabbos a delight,"
for the matter of delight
(of love with delights and of Shabbos)
is connected to the matter of rest,
meaning that there is then no aspect of toil,
as explained in Tanya
that the matter of love with delights is analogous to the reward, etc.,
however, the service,
from the term "processing of hides,"
and the service of the weekdays,
the general aspect of these services is through great toil and labor.
